summary: Extends the Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol so that destinations can be identified by a link identifier. The core specification assumes every modem has an attached DLEP router and identifies destinations by MAC address, which does not fit all radio networks.

eli5.summary: In the old way, each friend was named by a hardware address. This lets a modem use a different name tag when that does not fit.

questions: what is the dlep link identifier extension
how does dlep identify layer 3 destinations
subtitle: How a DLEP modem can describe links to destinations that sit beyond a gateway, not just on the local Layer 2 network.

tldr.problem: Core DLEP identifies every destination by the MAC address of an attached DLEP router, which does not fit modems that provide Layer 3 connectivity or reach destinations beyond a gateway.
tldr.mechanism: This extension adds a Link Identifier Data Item that is sent alongside the Gateway Node's MAC address, plus an optional Link Identifier Length Data Item to change the default 4-octet identifier size.
tldr.outcome: A router can learn link quality for Layer 3 destinations and use it in routing and flow-control decisions, as long as both peers announce the Link Identifiers extension (value 3) during session setup.

today: RFC 8703 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2020. It is not obsoleted or updated by any other RFC listed in the metadata, and it extends the core protocol in RFC 8175.

sections.title: Why Link Identifiers Exist
sections.content:
The Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP) lets modems tell attached routers about the state and quality of wireless links. The core specification, RFC 8175, assumes every modem in the radio network has an attached DLEP router, and it requires the MAC address of that router's DLEP interface to identify each destination.

RFC 8703 describes an extension for modems that do not meet that strict requirement. It lets them describe link availability and quality to one or more destinations reachable beyond a device on the Layer 2 domain. As with core DLEP, the router can use this knowledge to influence routing or flow-control decisions, understanding that the traffic flows via Layer 3.
sections.eli5: The old rule said every friend must be named by a hardware address. That does not work for friends who live behind another house, so this gives the radio a way to name them anyway.

sections.title: Terminology and Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC defines three terms. The local Layer 2 domain links the router and modem of the current DLEP session. A Layer 3 DLEP Destination is a destination that cannot be addressed directly in that domain but is reachable through a node that can. The Gateway Node is the last device with a MAC address on the path from the router towards that destination. It is commonly the DLEP peer modem, but could be another DLEP Destination in the Layer 2 domain.

The extension was designed mainly for three cases: a radio system that provides Layer 3 connectivity instead of running in Layer 2 bridge mode, a point-to-multipoint tunnel system such as an SD-WAN where the tunnel provider acts as a modem, and a modem such as an LTE device or 802.11 station that links to a remote wide-area network where a Layer 2 reachable remote router does not apply. The RFC says this list is not exhaustive.
sections.eli5: The gateway is the front door of a building, and the Layer 3 destination is a person inside. You can only find the door's address, so you also need a label for the person.

sections.title: How Destinations Are Referred To
sections.content:
To refer to a Layer 3 DLEP Destination, a participant adds a Link Identifier Data Item to the relevant Destination Message and, as usual, includes a MAC Address Data Item. Paired with a Link Identifier, the MAC address MUST be that of the Gateway Node. When the router wants to send a packet to the destination through the modem network, it MUST use the Gateway Node's MAC address as the Layer 2 destination.

Only modems know about Layer 3 destinations at first, so a new link MUST first appear in a Destination Up Message from modem to router. A router MUST NOT send a Destination Announce Message with a Link Identifier for a link not mentioned in an earlier Destination Up Message. A modem that receives one MUST terminate the session with a Session Termination Message carrying status code 131 ('Invalid Destination'). If a router receives a Destination Up Message that reuses an existing Link Identifier, it MUST answer with a Destination Up Response Message carrying status code 130 ('Invalid Data') and move to the Session Termination state.

Because the MAC address is not the final destination's address, every Destination Up Message with a Link Identifier MUST carry Layer 3 information: IPv4 or IPv6 Address Data Items, or Attached Subnet Data Items such as 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 for upstream backbone networks. Addresses MUST be those used on the public side of any Network Address Translation. Implementations SHOULD also announce at least one valid IP address of the Gateway Node, so the router need not run an extra address resolution protocol before adding the route.
sections.eli5: You write the front door's address on the envelope, and then add a name tag for the person inside. If someone mentions a name tag nobody has introduced, the radio hangs up the call.

sections.title: Identifier Rules and Negotiation
sections.content:
A Link Identifier is, by default, 4 octets long. A modem that wants a different length announces it with the Link Identifier Length Data Item in its Session Initialization Response Message, and the length MUST stay constant for the whole session. How identifiers are generated is a modem implementation matter, and routers must not assume anything about their meaning.

Within one session, identifiers MUST be unique per MAC address, so a Layer 3 destination is identified by the pair {MAC Address, Link Identifier}. A pair MUST NOT be reused within the lifetime of a single DLEP peer-to-peer session.

As with all DLEP extensions, support is announced at session initialization. A router includes value 3 ('Link Identifiers') in the Extension Data Item of its Session Initialization Message, and a modem does the same in its Session Initialization Response Message. Only if both advertise it can Link Identifier Data Items be used. If a modem needs the extension but the router did not advertise it, the modem MUST NOT send Link Identifier Data Items, and SHOULD NOT immediately end the session. It SHOULD use Session Messages and Attached Subnet Data Items to give general information instead.
sections.eli5: Both sides must say 'I know about name tags' before using them. Each tag must be used for one person only, and never handed out again during the same visit.

sections.title: The Two New Data Items
sections.content:
The extension adds two DLEP Data Items. The Link Identifier Length Data Item (type 26) has a Length of 2 and carries one field, the length in octets of Link Identifiers for this session. It is used only in the Session Initialization Response Message, only if the router advertised support, and only if the length is not the default of 4. A router that did not advertise support means it MUST NOT be sent. An item that specifies 4 octets is valid even though it has no effect.

The Link Identifier Data Item (type 27) carries the unique identifier of the Layer 3 DLEP Destination. Its Length is 4 by default, or whatever length was announced at session initialization. The identifier has no implicit meaning and is only used to tell links apart. It MAY be used wherever core DLEP allows a MAC Address Data Item.
sections.eli5: One note says how long the name tags will be. The other is the name tag itself, which is just a label so you can tell the links apart.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC adds no security mechanisms of its own. Since it extends core DLEP, the security considerations of RFC 8175 apply, and the document states that none of the features it introduces require extra security considerations from an implementation.
sections.eli5: This add-on does not change how safe the system is. The same safety rules as before still apply.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA assigned value 3 ('Link Identifiers') in the Extension Type Values registry, and types 26 ('Link Identifier Length') and 27 ('Link Identifier') in the Data Item Type Values registry. Both registries sit within the Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP) Parameters registry, and the new values fall in the range with the 'Specification Required' policy.
sections.eli5: The official number list now has three new entries, so nobody else picks the same numbers.
